title: Isolation Without a Commit Is Not a Backup

questions.prompt: An agent works in its own worktree, edits six files, runs the tests, and reports success. You check its branch with `git log --oneline main..worktree-agent` and get no output. The folder clearly has changes. What is the state of the branch?
options: The branch has commits, but `main` already contains them
The agent committed to `main` by mistake
The branch label still points where it started, so it has no commits of its own — the edits are uncommitted in the folder
questions.explanation: An empty range means the branch is where it started; the edits live only in the folder because nothing was committed. Option A is the tempting wrong answer because an empty range can also mean 'main already has it' — but that requires the commits to exist on the branch, which the dirty folder contradicts. The branch exists (you listed it), and if the agent had committed to `main`, `main` itself would show the changes.

questions.prompt: Before merging any finished agent branch, which pair of checks most directly reveals the empty-branch bug?
options: `git status` on main, and `git branch` on the worktree
questions.explanation: The signature is an empty commit range paired with a non-empty worktree status — nothing to merge, yet real work in the folder. Option C is the tempting wrong answer because `git worktree list` confirms a worktree exists, which feels like proof of work, but existence says nothing about commits. Tags and remote URLs are unrelated to whether a branch is empty.

questions.prompt: Two agents finish. Agent A committed everything before its worktree was removed; Agent B did not, and its worktree was removed by a sweep. Which work can git still recover, and with what?
options: Both — `git reflog` sees all edits that ever existed on disk
Only B — an agent worktree is backed up when it is swept
Only A — its commit is in the shared object store; B's edits were never committed and are gone
Neither — removing a worktree discards any commits it held
questions.explanation: A commit is written to the shared object store and survives the folder; uncommitted edits exist only in the folder and die with it. Option A is the tempting wrong answer because reflog sounds like it records everything — but it records *committed* positions of refs, never uncommitted file content. Agent A's commits are not discarded by worktree removal, so option D is also false.

questions.prompt: A colleague wants a durable fix so this cannot happen again, not just a note to 'remember to commit'. Which response matches the lesson?
options: Add a warning comment to the agent's prompt that says 'please commit soon'
Add a check — a hook or script — that fails when the worktree has uncommitted work at the end of the run
Disable worktrees entirely and run all agents in the main folder
Increase the worktree cleanup period so nothing is ever swept
questions.explanation: A guardrail that fires on uncommitted work is the fix, because the failure is silent and the forgetting agent is the one who cannot be trusted to remember. Option A is the tempting wrong answer because a stronger instruction feels like enforcement — but prose is a request, not a check, and this is exactly the failure mode of instructions. Disabling worktrees throws away isolation, and extending cleanup only delays the loss.
